claim: The Akap7 gene encodes multiple isoforms using two separate promoters to generate either long (γ/δ) or short (α) isoforms.
source: The Akap7 gene encodes multiple isoforms using two separate promoters to generate either long (γ/δ) or short (α) isoforms (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and shown in Figure 1A which displays the gene structure and resulting protein isoforms.

claim: Only the final exon of Akap7, containing the PKA-binding domain characteristic of AKAPs, is shared by all AKAP7 isoforms.
source: Only the final exon, containing the PKA-binding domain characteristic of AKAPs, is shared by all AKAP7 isoforms.
evidence: Directly stated in the text describing the gene structure.

claim: The final exon of Akap7 contains a modified leucine zipper domain which interacts with brain Na+ and L-type Ca2+ channels and facilitates PKA modulation of ion conductance through these channels.
source: The final exon also contains a modified leucine zipper domain which interacts with brain Na+ and L-type Ca2+ channels and facilitates PKA modulation of ion conductance through these channels (Marshall et al., 2011; Tibbs et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Marshall et al., 2011 and Tibbs et al., 1998.

claim: Long AKAP7 isoforms (γ/δ) are predominantly cytosolic.
source: Long isoforms, γ/δ, are predominantly cytosolic, although they contain a potential nuclear localization sequence.
evidence: Directly stated in the text describing isoform localization.

claim: Long AKAP7 isoforms contain a potential nuclear localization sequence.
source: Long isoforms, γ/δ, are predominantly cytosolic, although they contain a potential nuclear localization sequence.
evidence: Directly stated in the text describing isoform characteristics.

claim: Only the short α isoform of AKAP7 contains N-terminal myristoylation and palmitoylation sites.
source: Only the short α isoform contains N-terminal myristoylation and palmitoylation sites, facilitating plasma membrane association (Gray et al., 1998).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Gray et al., 1998.

claim: N-terminal myristoylation and palmitoylation sites facilitate plasma membrane association of AKAP7α.
source: Only the short α isoform contains N-terminal myristoylation and palmitoylation sites, facilitating plasma membrane association (Gray et al., 1998).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by citation to Gray et al., 1998.

claim: Long AKAP7 isoforms are expressed in all tissues examined including brain.
source: The long isoforms are expressed in all tissues examined including brain but the short isoform is predominantly expressed in neurons (Jones et al., 2012) and found in many regions of the brain including the hippocampus, cortex, striatum, thalamus and cerebellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Jones et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The short AKAP7 isoform is predominantly expressed in neurons.
source: The long isoforms are expressed in all tissues examined including brain but the short isoform is predominantly expressed in neurons (Jones et al., 2012) and found in many regions of the brain including the hippocampus, cortex, striatum, thalamus and cerebellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Jones et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AKAP7 is found in many regions of the brain including the hippocampus, cortex, striatum, thalamus and cerebellum.
source: The long isoforms are expressed in all tissues examined including brain but the short isoform is predominantly expressed in neurons (Jones et al., 2012) and found in many regions of the brain including the hippocampus, cortex, striatum, thalamus and cerebellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Jones et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The α isoform of AKAP7 is much more abundant than γ/δ in the hippocampus.
source: Western immunoblotting demonstrated that the α isoform is much more abundant than γ/δ in the hippocampus (Figure 1B) as well as other brain regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dentate granule cells specifically express AKAP7α and not AKAP7γ/δ.
source: We used RiboTag polyribosome immunoprecipitation (Sanz et al., 2009) to isolate DGC-specific polysome-associated mRNA from hippocampal homogenates to demonstrate that DGCs specifically express AKAP7α and not AKAP7γ/δ (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated using RiboTag method with results shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The global AKAP7 KO results in complete loss of both the long and short isoforms of AKAP7.
source: Western blot analysis of hippocampal extracts from WT and AKAP7 KO mice demonstrate the complete loss of both the long and short isoforms of AKAP7 with no change in the expression level of RIIβ (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The global AKAP7 KO does not change the expression level of PKA-RIIβ in the hippocampus.
source: Western blot analysis of hippocampal extracts from WT and AKAP7 KO mice demonstrate the complete loss of both the long and short isoforms of AKAP7 with no change in the expression level of RIIβ (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: AKAP7 is specifically expressed in dentate granule cells within the hippocampus.
source: Immunohistochemistry (Figure 1D) revealed the specific expression of AKAP7 in WT DGCs, the localization of AKAP7 protein to the MF projections and dendrites, and the complete loss of AKAP7 expression in the KO.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AKAP7 protein localizes to mossy fiber projections and dendrites.
source: Immunohistochemistry (Figure 1D) revealed the specific expression of AKAP7 in WT DGCs, the localization of AKAP7 protein to the MF projections and dendrites, and the complete loss of AKAP7 expression in the KO.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The global KO of AKAP7 did not disrupt the overall structure of the hippocampus.
source: The global KO of AKAP7 did not disrupt the overall structure of the hippocampus and the MF projections remain intact as shown by immunohistochemistry for zinc transporter-3 (ZNT3), a marker for MF terminals (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry for ZNT3 shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mossy fiber projections remain intact in the AKAP7 KO.
source: The global KO of AKAP7 did not disrupt the overall structure of the hippocampus and the MF projections remain intact as shown by immunohistochemistry for zinc transporter-3 (ZNT3), a marker for MF terminals (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry for ZNT3 shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the hippocampus, the short form of AKAP7 (AKAP7α) is preferentially expressed in dentate granule cells and localizes to both dendrites and the mossy fiber axonal projections.
source: Our results demonstrate that in the hippocampus, the short form of AKAP7 (AKAP7α) is preferentially expressed in DGCs and localizes to both dendrites and the MF axonal projections.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: AKAP7 co-localizes with neurofilament-M (NF-M), a protein found in axons.
source: AKAP7 co-localized with neurofilament-M (NF-M), a protein found in axons, and with ZNT3 and synaptophysin (SYP), which are present in MF boutons.
evidence: Stated in text describing colocalization experiments.

claim: AKAP7 co-localizes with ZNT3 and synaptophysin (SYP), which are present in mossy fiber boutons.
source: AKAP7 co-localized with neurofilament-M (NF-M), a protein found in axons, and with ZNT3 and synaptophysin (SYP), which are present in MF boutons.
evidence: Stated in text describing colocalization experiments.

claim: AKAP7 does not co-localize with post-synaptic density-95 (PSD-95).
source: We saw no co-localization of AKAP7 with markers for the post-synaptic density, post-synaptic density-95 (PSD-95), or dendrites, microtubule associated protein-2 (MAP-2), indicating that AKAP7 is localized in the MFs and not the CA3 dendrites (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: AKAP7 does not co-localize with microtubule associated protein-2 (MAP-2).
source: We saw no co-localization of AKAP7 with markers for the post-synaptic density, post-synaptic density-95 (PSD-95), or dendrites, microtubule associated protein-2 (MAP-2), indicating that AKAP7 is localized in the MFs and not the CA3 dendrites (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: AKAP7 is localized in the mossy fibers and not the CA3 dendrites.
source: We saw no co-localization of AKAP7 with markers for the post-synaptic density, post-synaptic density-95 (PSD-95), or dendrites, microtubule associated protein-2 (MAP-2), indicating that AKAP7 is localized in the MFs and not the CA3 dendrites (Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from lack of colocalization with postsynaptic markers, shown in Figure 2.

claim: AKAP7α is localized throughout mossy fiber boutons and axons.
source: Together, our data indicate that AKAP7α is localized throughout MF boutons and axons, identifying it as the only known presynaptic AKAP in mature neurons.
evidence: Summary statement based on colocalization data.

claim: AKAP7 is the only known presynaptic AKAP in mature neurons.
source: Together, our data indicate that AKAP7α is localized throughout MF boutons and axons, identifying it as the only known presynaptic AKAP in mature neurons.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the data and existing knowledge.

claim: Deletion of AKAP7 results in delocalization of PKA-RIIβ from the mossy fiber projections.
source: Deletion of AKAP7 resulted in delocalization of PKA-RIIβ from the MF projections as shown in Figure 3A and B.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Delocalization of PKA-RIIβ in the AKAP7 KO is not due to changes in overall PKA-RIIβ protein levels.
source: This was not due to changes in overall PKA-RIIβ protein levels (Figure 1B) but rather delocalization of PKA-RIIβ back to the cell body and dendrites of DGCs.
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: In the AKAP7 KO, PKA-RIIβ is delocalized back to the cell body and dendrites of dentate granule cells.
source: This was not due to changes in overall PKA-RIIβ protein levels (Figure 1B) but rather delocalization of PKA-RIIβ back to the cell body and dendrites of DGCs.
evidence: Stated in text describing the redistribution of PKA-RIIβ.

claim: AKAP7 is the sole AKAP anchoring PKA-RIIβ in mossy fiber axons.
source: This result strongly suggests that AKAP7 is the sole AKAP anchoring PKA-RIIβ in MF axons.
evidence: Inferred from the complete delocalization of PKA-RIIβ from MF axons in the AKAP7 KO.

claim: Most of the PKA catalytic subunit is displaced from the stratum lucidum in the AKAP7 KO.
source: Staining for the catalytic subunit, PKA-C, revealed that most of the C subunit was also displaced from the stratum lucidum in the AKAP7 KO and what remained did not colocalize with NF-M suggesting that the remaining C subunit was in CA3 pyramidal cells, interneurons, or glia (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The remaining PKA-C in the stratum lucidum of AKAP7 KO does not colocalize with NF-M.
source: Staining for the catalytic subunit, PKA-C, revealed that most of the C subunit was also displaced from the stratum lucidum in the AKAP7 KO and what remained did not colocalize with NF-M suggesting that the remaining C subunit was in CA3 pyramidal cells, interneurons, or glia (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The remaining PKA-C in the stratum lucidum of AKAP7 KO is likely in CA3 pyramidal cells, interneurons, or glia.
source: Staining for the catalytic subunit, PKA-C, revealed that most of the C subunit was also displaced from the stratum lucidum in the AKAP7 KO and what remained did not colocalize with NF-M suggesting that the remaining C subunit was in CA3 pyramidal cells, interneurons, or glia (Figure 3C).
evidence: Inferred from lack of colocalization with axonal marker NF-M.

claim: AKAP7 is required for localization of the PKA holoenzyme to mossy fiber axons and terminals.
source: Thus, AKAP7 is required for localization of the PKA holoenzyme to MF axons and terminals.
evidence: Conclusion based on delocalization of both regulatory and catalytic subunits in the KO.

claim: The MF-CA3 synapse expresses a form of presynaptic, PKA-dependent, and NMDA receptor-independent LTP.
source: The MF-CA3 synapse is well-known for expressing a form of presynaptic, PKA-dependent, and NMDA receptor-independent LTP (herein referred to as MF-LTP) (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005.

claim: Cyclic AMP-induced LTP was nearly abolished in AKAP7 KO mice when compared to WT littermate controls.
source: Cyclic AMP-induced LTP, monitored with extracellular field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP) recordings, was nearly abolished in the AKAP7 KO mice when compared to WT littermate controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: cAMP-induced MF-LTP was severely reduced in AKAP7 KO mice compared with WT controls as measured by whole-cell recordings.
source: Consistent with our field recording measurements, cAMP-induced MF-LTP was severely reduced in AKAP7 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-cell electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tetanus-induced LTP remained intact in the AKAP7 KO mice.
source: Intriguingly, tetanus-induced LTP remained intact in the AKAP7 KO mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tetanus-induced LTP in AKAP7 KO slices remains dependent on PKA.
source: We pharmacologically inhibited PKA with H89 and observed that the tetanus-induced LTP in AKAP7 KO slices remained dependent on PKA (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition experiment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Presynaptic long-term depression (LTD) at MF-CA3 synapses relies on cAMP/PKA signaling.
source: A previous report found that presynaptic long-term depression (LTD) at MF-CA3 synapses also relies on cAMP/PKA signaling (Tzounopoulos et al., 1998).
evidence: Stated with citation to Tzounopoulos et al., 1998.

claim: LTD was preserved in the AKAP7 KO mice compared with WT controls.
source: We therefore examined the AKAP7 KO and found that LTD was preserved in the AKAP7 KO mice compared with WT controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: All measured short-term plasticity dynamics (paired-pulse facilitation and frequency facilitation) were comparable to WT controls in AKAP7 KO mice.
source: All measured short-term plasticity dynamics, paired-pulse facilitation (Figure 4G) and frequency facilitation (Figure 4H and I) were comparable to WT controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 4G, H, and I.

claim: Deletion of AKAP7 does not cause gross changes in basal synaptic function.
source: These results are consistent with our anatomical findings that deletion of AKAP7 does not cause gross changes in basal synaptic function.
evidence: Inferred from normal short-term plasticity and anatomical findings.

claim: cAMP-induced LTP requires high levels of localized PKA signaling in mossy fiber axons and presynaptic terminals.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that cAMP-induced LTP requires high levels of localized PKA signaling in MF axons and presynaptic terminals, whereas tetanus-induced LTP does not.
evidence: Conclusion based on differential effects of AKAP7 deletion on cAMP-induced versus tetanus-induced LTP.

claim: Tetanus-induced LTP does not require high levels of localized PKA signaling in mossy fiber axons and presynaptic terminals.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that cAMP-induced LTP requires high levels of localized PKA signaling in MF axons and presynaptic terminals, whereas tetanus-induced LTP does not.
evidence: Conclusion based on differential effects of AKAP7 deletion on cAMP-induced versus tetanus-induced LTP.

claim: Disruption of DG function in mice impairs contextual and non-cued spatial forms of discrimination (pattern separation).
source: Disruption of DG function in mice has been shown to impair contextual (McHugh et al., 2007) and non-cued spatial forms of discrimination (Gilbert et al., 1998), commonly referred to as pattern separation.
evidence: Stated with citations to McHugh et al., 2007 and Gilbert et al., 1998.

claim: WT mice demonstrated intact contextual pattern separation by rapidly learning that context B was comparatively safer and reducing their freezing behavior in context B after just one trial.
source: WT mice demonstrated intact contextual pattern separation because they rapidly learned that context B was comparatively safer and reduced their freezing behavior in context B after just one trial while retaining a robust freezing response in context A.
evidence: Stated in text describing behavioral results.

claim: AKAP7 KO mice took 7–8 trials to distinguish context B from context A in the contextual fear discrimination paradigm.
source: However, AKAP7 KO mice took 7–8 trials to distinguish context B from context A (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: AKAP7 KO mice were slightly delayed in extinction of freezing behavior.
source: The AKAP7 KO mice were also slightly delayed in extinction of freezing behavior (Figure 5E), which is thought to involve inhibitory learning (Myers and Davis, 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 5E, with citation to Myers and Davis, 2007 for interpretation.

claim: AKAP7 KO mice were not impaired in a typical contextual memory task (Barnes maze).
source: Apart from these behavioral differences, KO mice were not impaired in a typical contextual memory task (Barnes maze) and did not display changes in anxiety as assessed by elevated plus maze, open field and marble burying (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AKAP7 KO mice did not display changes in anxiety as assessed by elevated plus maze, open field and marble burying.
source: Apart from these behavioral differences, KO mice were not impaired in a typical contextual memory task (Barnes maze) and did not display changes in anxiety as assessed by elevated plus maze, open field and marble burying (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no differences in gross motor function in AKAP7 KO mice as measured by wire hang, pole test, and rotarod.
source: There were also no differences in gross motor function as measured by wire hang, pole test, and rotarod (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AKAP7 plays a crucial role in DG-mediated contextual pattern separation without significant effects on other common behavioral paradigms.
source: These results suggest that AKAP7 plays a crucial role in DG-mediated contextual pattern separation without significant effects on other common behavioral paradigms.
evidence: Conclusion based on selective behavioral deficits in pattern separation tasks but not other behavioral tests.

claim: Pattern separation behavior has been directly linked to the process of ongoing neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the DG.
source: Pattern separation behavior has been directly linked to the process of ongoing neurogenesis that occurs in the subgranular zone of the DG leading to a continuous integration of adult-born DGCs into the hippocampal circuit.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inhibition of neurogenesis by irradiation results in impaired pattern separation.
source: Inhibition of neurogenesis by irradiation (Clelland et al., 2009) or by using genetic approaches (Nakashiba et al., 2012; Scobie et al., 2009; Tronel et al., 2012) results in impaired pattern separation, whereas increasing neurogenesis leads to improved performance in a pattern separation assay (Creer et al., 2010; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Inhibition of neurogenesis by genetic approaches results in impaired pattern separation.
source: Inhibition of neurogenesis by irradiation (Clelland et al., 2009) or by using genetic approaches (Nakashiba et al., 2012; Scobie et al., 2009; Tronel et al., 2012) results in impaired pattern separation, whereas increasing neurogenesis leads to improved performance in a pattern separation assay (Creer et al., 2010; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Increasing neurogenesis leads to improved performance in a pattern separation assay.
source: Inhibition of neurogenesis by irradiation (Clelland et al., 2009) or by using genetic approaches (Nakashiba et al., 2012; Scobie et al., 2009; Tronel et al., 2012) results in impaired pattern separation, whereas increasing neurogenesis leads to improved performance in a pattern separation assay (Creer et al., 2010; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations to Creer et al., 2010 and Sahay et al., 2011.

claim: There were no differences in adult neurogenesis between WT and AKAP7 KO mice under basal conditions.
source: We found no differences in adult neurogenesis either under basal conditions or when enhanced by running wheel access and environmental enrichment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no differences in adult neurogenesis between WT and AKAP7 KO mice when enhanced by running wheel access and environmental enrichment.
source: We found no differences in adult neurogenesis either under basal conditions or when enhanced by running wheel access and environmental enrichment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is unlikely that reduced neurogenesis underlies the deficits in contextual pattern separation behavior observed in the AKAP7 KO mice.
source: It is therefore unlikely that reduced neurogenesis underlies the deficits in contextual pattern separation behavior that we observe in the AKAP7 KO mice.
evidence: Conclusion based on normal neurogenesis in the AKAP7 KO.

claim: TdTomato expression in Pomc-Cre mice crossed to TdTomato reporter mice was tightly restricted to DGCs and the arcuate nucleus.
source: Specificity of Cre recombinase expression was determined by TdTomato reporter (ROSA26Sor-lox-STOP-TdTomato x Pomc-Cre) (Figure 6A–B). TdTomato expression was tightly restricted to DGCs and the arcuate nucleus, consistent with previous reports (McHugh et al., 2007; Sanz et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated by TdTomato reporter expression shown in Figures 6A-B, with citations to previous reports.

claim: DG-KO animals lose AKAP7 in the dentate gyrus but not the neighboring thalamus.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed delocalization of PKA-RIIβ and loss of AKAP7 in the DGCs of DG-KO animals, whereas localization and expression in Het animals were normal (Figure 6C). Expression of AKAP7 in the thalamus (Figure 6C) and other brain regions was unaffected in the DG-KO.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PKA-RIIβ is displaced from mossy fibers in DG-KO animals.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed delocalization of PKA-RIIβ and loss of AKAP7 in the DGCs of DG-KO animals, whereas localization and expression in Het animals were normal (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AKAP7 detected in the DG molecular layer in WT mice arises from DGCs and not axonal projections of the perforant path.
source: These results further demonstrate that the AKAP7 detected in the DG molecular layer in WT mice arises from DGCs and not axonal projections of the perforant path.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of AKAP7 in the molecular layer in DG-specific KO.

claim: DG-KO mice exhibited an impairment in cAMP-induced LTP.
source: The DG-KO mice exhibited an impairment in cAMP-induced LTP, although the decrease was not as complete as in the global AKAP7 KO (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The impairment in cAMP-induced LTP in DG-KO mice was not as complete as in the global AKAP7 KO.
source: The DG-KO mice exhibited an impairment in cAMP-induced LTP, although the decrease was not as complete as in the global AKAP7 KO (Figure 6D). This likely results from some residual levels of AKAP7 and RIIβ present in the MF pathway due to incomplete Cre recombination.
evidence: Stated in text with explanation, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Residual levels of AKAP7 and RIIβ in the MF pathway of DG-KO mice are due to incomplete Cre recombination.
source: This likely results from some residual levels of AKAP7 and RIIβ present in the MF pathway due to incomplete Cre recombination.
evidence: Stated as explanation for partial phenotype in DG-KO.

claim: Synaptically-induced LTP remained intact in the DG-KO.
source: As in the global KO, the synaptically-induced LTP remained intact in the DG-KO (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Presynaptically localized AKAP7 and its anchored PKA-RIIβ are essential for cAMP-induced LTP.
source: These results confirm that presynaptically localized AKAP7 and its anchored PKA-RIIβ are essential for cAMP-induced LTP.
evidence: Conclusion based on DG-specific KO recapitulating the cAMP-induced LTP deficit.

claim: AKAP7 global KO and DG-KO animals committed significantly more errors in the 2-arm configuration of the DNMP test compared to WT and Het over the 5-day experiment.
source: AKAP7 KO and DG-KO animals committed significantly more errors in the 2-arm configuration compared to WT and Het over the 5-day experiment (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the 4-arm separation task, AKAP7 KO and DG-KO animals performed similar to WT and Het animals during the fourth and fifth day of training.
source: In the 4-arm separation task, AKAP7 KO and DG-KO animals performed similar to WT and Het animals during the fourth and fifth day of training.
evidence: Stated in text describing behavioral results.

claim: The specific loss of AKAP7 from DGCs was sufficient to disrupt non-cued spatial pattern separation to the same degree as observed for the global KO when animals were challenged in the 2-arm test.
source: Critically, the specific loss of AKAP7 from DGCs was sufficient to disrupt non-cued spatial pattern separation to the same degree as observed for the global KO when animals were challenged in the 2-arm test (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Defective pattern separation is directly linked to AKAP7 function in DGCs.
source: These results demonstrate that defective pattern separation is directly linked to AKAP7 function in DGCs.
evidence: Conclusion based on DG-specific KO recapitulating the behavioral deficit of the global KO.

claim: AKAP7 is the first presynaptic AKAP involved in anchoring PKA in axonal projections in adult neurons.
source: Our study has identified the first presynaptic AKAP involved in anchoring PKA in axonal projections in adult neurons.
evidence: Summary statement of the main finding.

claim: AKAP7α localizes PKA-RIIβ presynaptically in the axons and terminals of MF projections to the CA3 pyramidal cells of the hippocampus.
source: AKAP7α localizes PKA-RIIβ presynaptically in the axons and terminals of MF projections to the CA3 pyramidal cells of the hippocampus.
evidence: Summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Loss of AKAP7 impairs the localization of PKA in the MF projections.
source: We find that loss of AKAP7 impairs the localization of PKA in the MF projections and leads to a defect in pattern separation behaviors that have been shown to depend specifically on DGCs (McHugh et al., 2007).
evidence: Summary statement of findings with citation to McHugh et al., 2007.

claim: Loss of AKAP7 leads to a defect in pattern separation behaviors that depend specifically on DGCs.
source: We find that loss of AKAP7 impairs the localization of PKA in the MF projections and leads to a defect in pattern separation behaviors that have been shown to depend specifically on DGCs (McHugh et al., 2007).
evidence: Summary statement of findings with citation to McHugh et al., 2007.

claim: The AKAP7 KO displays a dramatic loss of cAMP-induced LTP at the MF-CA3 synapse.
source: In addition, we find that the AKAP7 KO displays a dramatic loss of cAMP-induced LTP at the MF-CA3 synapse.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: Presynaptic PKA plays an important functional role in synaptic plasticity at hippocampal MF-CA3 synapses.
source: There are multiple circuits in which presynaptic PKA has been shown to play an important functional role in synaptic plasticity including the hippocampal MF-CA3 synapses (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), the hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapse (Park et al., 2014), cortico-thalamic synapses (Castro-Alamancos and Calcagnotto, 1999), corticostriatal synapses (Spencer and Murphy, 2002) and the parallel fiber synapses in the cerebellum (Salin et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005.

claim: Presynaptic PKA plays an important functional role in synaptic plasticity at the hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapse.
source: There are multiple circuits in which presynaptic PKA has been shown to play an important functional role in synaptic plasticity including the hippocampal MF-CA3 synapses (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), the hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapse (Park et al., 2014), cortico-thalamic synapses (Castro-Alamancos and Calcagnotto, 1999), corticostriatal synapses (Spencer and Murphy, 2002) and the parallel fiber synapses in the cerebellum (Salin et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Park et al., 2014.

claim: Presynaptic PKA plays an important functional role in synaptic plasticity at cortico-thalamic synapses.
source: There are multiple circuits in which presynaptic PKA has been shown to play an important functional role in synaptic plasticity including the hippocampal MF-CA3 synapses (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), the hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapse (Park et al., 2014), cortico-thalamic synapses (Castro-Alamancos and Calcagnotto, 1999), corticostriatal synapses (Spencer and Murphy, 2002) and the parallel fiber synapses in the cerebellum (Salin et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Castro-Alamancos and Calcagnotto, 1999.

claim: Presynaptic PKA plays an important functional role in synaptic plasticity at corticostriatal synapses.
source: There are multiple circuits in which presynaptic PKA has been shown to play an important functional role in synaptic plasticity including the hippocampal MF-CA3 synapses (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), the hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapse (Park et al., 2014), cortico-thalamic synapses (Castro-Alamancos and Calcagnotto, 1999), corticostriatal synapses (Spencer and Murphy, 2002) and the parallel fiber synapses in the cerebellum (Salin et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Spencer and Murphy, 2002.

claim: Presynaptic PKA plays an important functional role in synaptic plasticity at parallel fiber synapses in the cerebellum.
source: There are multiple circuits in which presynaptic PKA has been shown to play an important functional role in synaptic plasticity including the hippocampal MF-CA3 synapses (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), the hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapse (Park et al., 2014), cortico-thalamic synapses (Castro-Alamancos and Calcagnotto, 1999), corticostriatal synapses (Spencer and Murphy, 2002) and the parallel fiber synapses in the cerebellum (Salin et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Salin et al., 1996.

claim: In the hippocampus, AKAP7α is primarily restricted to DGCs.
source: In the hippocampus, AKAP7α is primarily restricted to DGCs, although it is expressed in other brain regions including the cortex, striatum, thalamus and cerebellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In MF axons, AKAP7 is apparently the only anchor for PKA-RIIβ.
source: In MF axons, AKAP7 is apparently the only anchor for PKA-RIIβ since the two proteins colocalize throughout the axons and terminals and the loss of AKAP7 results in delocalization of PKA-RIIβ and C subunits from these presynaptic projections as indicated by a strong reduction in immunofluorescence.
evidence: Inferred from complete colocalization and complete delocalization upon AKAP7 deletion.

claim: Dendritic PKA remains localized in the AKAP7 KO and is likely to bind other postsynaptic AKAPs including AKAP5, AKAP12 (gravin) and MAP2.
source: Dendritic PKA remains localized in the AKAP7 KO and is likely to bind other postsynaptic AKAPs including AKAP5 (Sanderson and Dell'Acqua, 2011; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010), AKAP12 (gravin) (Havekes et al., 2012) and MAP2 (Zhong et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Colchicine induced lesions in the DG, but not CA1 regions of the hippocampus in rats, produced deficits in spatial discrimination.
source: Early studies found that colchicine induced lesions in the DG, but not CA1 regions of the hippocampus in rats, produced deficits in spatial discrimination (Gilbert et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated with citation to Gilbert et al., 2001.

claim: Genetic disruption of the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor specifically in DGCs results in a defect in discrimination between similar contexts (pattern separation) in mice.
source: Genetic disruption of the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor specifically in DGCs results in a defect in discrimination between similar contexts (pattern separation) in mice (McHugh et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citation to McHugh et al., 2007.

claim: Adult born DGCs are preferentially involved in accurate pattern separation.
source: Although the mechanisms are not resolved, the studies indicate that adult born DGCs are preferentially involved in accurate pattern separation, and the mature DGCs are required for pattern completion or generalization (Danielson et al., 2016; Nakashiba et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to Danielson et al., 2016 and Nakashiba et al., 2012.

claim: Mature DGCs are required for pattern completion or generalization.
source: Although the mechanisms are not resolved, the studies indicate that adult born DGCs are preferentially involved in accurate pattern separation, and the mature DGCs are required for pattern completion or generalization (Danielson et al., 2016; Nakashiba et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to Danielson et al., 2016 and Nakashiba et al., 2012.

claim: Deleting AKAP7 did not affect adult neurogenesis.
source: We found that deleting AKAP7 did not affect adult neurogenesis, but the function of AKAP7 in pattern separation could preferentially involve these adult born DGCs.
evidence: Stated based on neurogenesis experiments.

claim: The function of AKAP7 in pattern separation could preferentially involve adult born DGCs.
source: We found that deleting AKAP7 did not affect adult neurogenesis, but the function of AKAP7 in pattern separation could preferentially involve these adult born DGCs.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism.

claim: MF-LTP can be induced by repeated trains of tetanic stimulation or direct activation of cyclases with forskolin to elevate cAMP.
source: MF-LTP can be induced by repeated trains of tetanic stimulation or direct activation of cyclases with forskolin to elevate cAMP.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: Bath application of PKA inhibitors during tetanus blocks the induction of MF-LTP.
source: Bath application of PKA inhibitors during tetanus blocks the induction of MF-LTP (Huang et al., 1994; Weisskopf et al., 1994).
evidence: Stated with citations to Huang et al., 1994 and Weisskopf et al., 1994.

claim: Deletion of AC1 or AC8 reduced tetanus-induced MF-LTP.
source: Deletion of AC1 or AC8 reduced tetanus-induced MF-LTP and the AC1/AC8 double KO completely eliminated tetanus induced LTP.
evidence: Stated as previous finding.

claim: The AC1/AC8 double KO completely eliminated tetanus induced LTP.
source: Deletion of AC1 or AC8 reduced tetanus-induced MF-LTP and the AC1/AC8 double KO completely eliminated tetanus induced LTP.
evidence: Stated as previous finding.

claim: LTP induced by direct cyclase activation with forskolin was unaffected in the AC1/AC8 double KO.
source: It is interesting to note that the LTP induced by direct cyclase activation with forskolin was unaffected in the AC1/AC8 double KO (Wong et al., 1999) suggesting that forskolin is acting on another cyclase in the DGCs to induce LTP.
evidence: Stated with citation to Wong et al., 1999.

claim: Forskolin is acting on another cyclase in the DGCs to induce LTP.
source: It is interesting to note that the LTP induced by direct cyclase activation with forskolin was unaffected in the AC1/AC8 double KO (Wong et al., 1999) suggesting that forskolin is acting on another cyclase in the DGCs to induce LTP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that forskolin-induced LTP is intact in AC1/AC8 double KO.

claim: Targeted disruption of either the Cβ or RIβ subunit gene of PKA inhibited tetanus-induced LTP at MF-CA3 synapses without decreasing cAMP-induced LTP.
source: Targeted disruption of either the Cβ or RIβ subunit gene of PKA inhibited tetanus-induced LTP at MF-CA3 synapses without decreasing cAMP-induced LTP (Huang et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated with citation to Huang et al., 1995.

claim: Epac2 KO mice demonstrate defects in both tetanus- and cAMP-induced MF-LTP.
source: Recently, the contribution of another cAMP effector, Epac2, was examined. Epac2 is a cAMP-regulated guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for Rap1/2, and electrophysiological recordings from Epac2 KO mice demonstrate defects in both tetanus- and cAMP-induced MF-LTP (Fernandes et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to Fernandes et al., 2015.

claim: Synaptically induced LTP may be more dependent on the axonal transport of synaptic vesicle proteins that might be phosphorylated in the soma and delivered to the terminals.
source: One possibility is that synaptically induced LTP is more dependent on the axonal transport of synaptic vesicle proteins that might be phosphorylated in the soma and delivered to the terminals.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differential LTP mechanisms.

claim: Rates for transport of Golgi-derived vesicles are as high as 2–5 µm/s.
source: Rates for transport of these Golgi-derived vesicles are as high as 2–5 µm/s (Brown, 2000), and they could therefore travel the ~1000 µm distance from the DGC body to the terminals and play a role in the sustained LTP seen 30–40 min after tetanic stimulation.
evidence: Stated with citation to Brown, 2000.

claim: Severing the MF axons near the DGC body prevents synaptically induced LTP without affecting cAMP-induced LTP.
source: Severing the MF axons near the DGC body prevents synaptically induced LTP without affecting cAMP-induced LTP further supporting a role for the cell body in maintenance of synaptically induced LTP (Calixto et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated with citation to Calixto et al., 2003.

claim: PKA-RI is typically concentrated in the soma of neurons.
source: RI and RII isoforms of PKA have different anchoring characteristics (Di Benedetto et al., 2008) with PKA-RI typically concentrated in the soma of neurons (Yang et al., 2014), while PKA-RIIβ is usually tightly anchored to AKAPs in dendrites and, in this study, axonal projections.
evidence: Stated with citations to Di Benedetto et al., 2008 and Yang et al., 2014.

claim: PKA-RIIβ is usually tightly anchored to AKAPs in dendrites and axonal projections.
source: RI and RII isoforms of PKA have different anchoring characteristics (Di Benedetto et al., 2008) with PKA-RI typically concentrated in the soma of neurons (Yang et al., 2014), while PKA-RIIβ is usually tightly anchored to AKAPs in dendrites and, in this study, axonal projections.
evidence: Stated with citations and based on findings in this study.

claim: Tetanus-induced LTP depends on PKA activation in the somatodendritic compartment.
source: This leads us to speculate that tetanus-induced LTP depends on PKA activation in the somatodendritic compartment and cAMP-induced LTP depends on PKA-RIIβ in the MF projections.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on the differential effects of AKAP7 deletion.

claim: cAMP-induced LTP depends on PKA-RIIβ in the MF projections.
source: This leads us to speculate that tetanus-induced LTP depends on PKA activation in the somatodendritic compartment and cAMP-induced LTP depends on PKA-RIIβ in the MF projections.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on the differential effects of AKAP7 deletion.

claim: There is evidence for synergism between the β-adrenergic receptor agonist, isoproterenol, and repetitive synaptic stimulation of MF-LTP in slice culture.
source: There is evidence for synergism between the β-adrenergic receptor agonist, isoproterenol, and repetitive synaptic stimulation of MF-LTP in slice culture (Huang and Kandel, 1996).
evidence: Stated with citation to Huang and Kandel, 1996.

claim: A weak tetanic stimulation of the MF-CA3 pathway in vivo can synergize with lateral ventricle administration of isoproterenol to elicit LTP lasting more than 24 hr.
source: More recently, it has been observed that a weak tetanic stimulation of the MF-CA3 pathway in vivo can synergize with lateral ventricle administration of isoproterenol to elicit LTP lasting more than 24 hr (Hagena and Manahan-Vaughan, 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation to Hagena and Manahan-Vaughan, 2012.

claim: The pituitary adenylate cyclase activating peptide (PACAP) receptor is highly expressed in DGCs.
source: In addition, the pituitary adenylate cyclase activating peptide (PACAP) receptor is highly expressed in DGCs and this Gs-coupled GPCR is localized to MF projections (Otto et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated with citation to Otto et al., 1999.

claim: The PACAP receptor is localized to MF projections.
source: In addition, the pituitary adenylate cyclase activating peptide (PACAP) receptor is highly expressed in DGCs and this Gs-coupled GPCR is localized to MF projections (Otto et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated with citation to Otto et al., 1999.

claim: Targeted disruption of the PACAP receptor (Adcyap1r1) in neocortex and hippocampus led to deficits in both MF-LTP and contextual fear conditioning.
source: Targeted disruption of the PACAP receptor (Adcyap1r1) in neocortex and hippocampus led to deficits in both MF-LTP and contextual fear conditioning (Otto et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated with citation to Otto et al., 2001.

claim: AKAP7-localized PKA provides an intracellular signaling mechanism to potentiate the actions of neuromodulators targeting G-protein-coupled receptors expressed specifically on the MF projections.
source: We propose that AKAP7-localized PKA provides an intracellular signaling mechanism to potentiate the actions of neuromodulators targeting G-protein-coupled receptors expressed specifically on the MF projections.
evidence: Proposed model based on the findings.

claim: DG dysfunction has been implicated in a wide range of psychiatric disorders including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and addictive behavior.
source: DG dysfunction has been implicated in a wide range of psychiatric disorders including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and addictive behavior (García-Fuster et al., 2013; Kheirbek et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to García-Fuster et al., 2013 and Kheirbek et al., 2012.

claim: Alterations in presynaptically anchored PKA can disrupt specific aspects of DG function and could play a role in psychiatric disorders.
source: Our studies suggest that alterations in presynaptically anchored PKA can disrupt specific aspects of DG function and could play a role in these disorders.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the findings.

claim: Protein Kinase A (PKA) mediates synaptic plasticity and is widely implicated in learning and memory.
source: Protein Kinase A (PKA) mediates synaptic plasticity and is widely implicated in learning and memory.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) is thought to be responsible for processing and encoding distinct contextual associations in response to highly similar inputs.
source: The hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) is thought to be responsible for processing and encoding distinct contextual associations in response to highly similar inputs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The mossy fiber (MF) axons of the dentate granule cells convey strong excitatory drive to CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: The mossy fiber (MF) axons of the dentate granule cells convey strong excitatory drive to CA3 pyramidal neurons and express presynaptic, PKA-dependent forms of plasticity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Mossy fiber axons express presynaptic, PKA-dependent forms of plasticity.
source: The mossy fiber (MF) axons of the dentate granule cells convey strong excitatory drive to CA3 pyramidal neurons and express presynaptic, PKA-dependent forms of plasticity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Genetic ablation of AKAP7 specifically from dentate granule cells results in disruption of MF-CA3 LTP directly initiated by cAMP.
source: Genetic ablation of AKAP7 specifically from dentate granule cells results in disruption of MF-CA3 LTP directly initiated by cAMP, and the AKAP7 mutant mice are selectively deficient in pattern separation behaviors.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract.

claim: AKAP7 mutant mice are selectively deficient in pattern separation behaviors.
source: Genetic ablation of AKAP7 specifically from dentate granule cells results in disruption of MF-CA3 LTP directly initiated by cAMP, and the AKAP7 mutant mice are selectively deficient in pattern separation behaviors.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract.

claim: The AKAP7/PKA complex in the MF projections plays an essential role in synaptic plasticity and contextual memory formation.
source: Our results suggest that the AKAP7/PKA complex in the MF projections plays an essential role in synaptic plasticity and contextual memory formation.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the abstract.

claim: The hippocampal formation plays a crucial role in the encoding and retrieval of episodic and spatial memories.
source: The hippocampal formation, which comprises the hippocampus and dentate gyrus (DG), plays a crucial role in the encoding and retrieval of episodic and spatial memories (Burgess et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation to Burgess et al., 2002.

claim: The DG receives input from the entorhinal cortex and sends its output via dentate granule cell (DGC) axons or mossy fibers (MFs) to synapse with proximal dendrites of hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: The DG receives input from the entorhinal cortex and sends its output via dentate granule cell (DGC) axons or mossy fibers (MFs) to synapse with proximal dendrites of hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (Amaral et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citation to Amaral et al., 2007.

claim: One function of the DG is to accurately separate similar memories by orthogonally encoding discrete non-overlapping input patterns onto the CA3 field.
source: Previous theoretical studies predicted that one function of the DG is to accurately separate similar memories by orthogonally encoding discrete non-overlapping input patterns onto the CA3 field (Lee and Solivan, 2010; Rolls, 2013; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to Lee and Solivan, 2010; Rolls, 2013; Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: This precise form of encoding is known as pattern separation.
source: This precise form of encoding is known as pattern separation (Gilbert et al., 2001; Kesner and Rolls, 2015; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Nakashiba et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Behavioral studies have helped to clarify the role of the circuit between the DG and region CA3 in modulating spatial and contextual pattern separation.
source: Behavioral studies have helped to clarify the role of the circuit between the DG and region CA3 in modulating spatial and contextual pattern separation (Aimone et al., 2011; Myers and Scharfman, 2011; Treves et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated with citations to Aimone et al., 2011; Myers and Scharfman, 2011; Treves et al., 2008.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to the functional role of the DG-CA3 circuit in pattern separation are incompletely understood.
source: However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to this functional role in pattern separation are incompletely understood.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Activity-dependent, long-term changes in synaptic transmission (e.g. long-term potentiation, LTP, and depression, LTD) within hippocampal circuits provide a basis for learning and memory.
source: Activity-dependent, long-term changes in synaptic transmission (e.g. long-term potentiation, LTP, and depression, LTD) within hippocampal circuits provide a basis for learning and memory.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: Protein Kinase A (PKA) is a key mediator of both pre- and postsynaptic forms of long-term plasticity.
source: Protein Kinase A (PKA) is a key mediator of both pre- and postsynaptic forms of long-term plasticity (Kandel et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citation to Kandel et al., 2014.

claim: A Kinase Anchoring Proteins (AKAPs) are multi-domain scaffolding proteins that localize PKA and other proteins to discrete subcellular domains.
source: A Kinase Anchoring Proteins (AKAPs) are multi-domain scaffolding proteins that localize PKA and other proteins to discrete subcellular domains and spatially restrict intracellular signaling events that are required for neuroplasticity (Dell'Acqua et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citations to Dell'Acqua et al., 2006 and Scott et al., 2013.

claim: AKAPs spatially restrict intracellular signaling events that are required for neuroplasticity.
source: A Kinase Anchoring Proteins (AKAPs) are multi-domain scaffolding proteins that localize PKA and other proteins to discrete subcellular domains and spatially restrict intracellular signaling events that are required for neuroplasticity (Dell'Acqua et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citations to Dell'Acqua et al., 2006 and Scott et al., 2013.

claim: Genetic deletion of AKAP5 results in delocalization of PKA from the postsynaptic dendrites of CA1 and CA3 hippocampal neurons.
source: We, and others, have shown that genetic deletion of a dendritic AKAP (AKAP5) results in delocalization of PKA from the postsynaptic dendrites of CA1 and CA3 hippocampal neurons and leads to behavioral defects in memory and learning (Lu et al., 2007; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citations to Lu et al., 2007; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010.

claim: Genetic deletion of AKAP5 leads to behavioral defects in memory and learning.
source: We, and others, have shown that genetic deletion of a dendritic AKAP (AKAP5) results in delocalization of PKA from the postsynaptic dendrites of CA1 and CA3 hippocampal neurons and leads to behavioral defects in memory and learning (Lu et al., 2007; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated with citations to Lu et al., 2007; Tunquist et al., 2008; Weisenhaus et al., 2010.

claim: Previous studies have shown localization of PKA-RIIβ to MF projections.
source: Previous studies have shown localization of PKA-RIIβ to MF projections (Glantz et al., 1992; Weisenhaus et al., 2010) suggesting the presence of a presynaptic anchoring protein.
evidence: Stated with citations to Glantz et al., 1992 and Weisenhaus et al., 2010.

claim: No presynaptic AKAP has been previously reported in adult neurons.
source: However, no presynaptic AKAP has been previously reported in adult neurons.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: A role for AKAPs in pattern separation has not been explored.
source: Moreover, a role for AKAPs in pattern separation has not been explored.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: A model for MF-LTP suggests that presynaptic calcium influx activates calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclases (ACs) that produce cyclic AMP (cAMP) leading to PKA activation and the phosphorylation of substrates.
source: A model for MF-LTP suggests that presynaptic calcium influx activates calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclases (ACs) that produce cyclic AMP (cAMP) leading to PKA activation and the phosphorylation of substrates (Huang et al., 1994; Villacres et al., 1998; Wang et al., 2003; Weisskopf et al., 1994).
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: MF-LTP can be induced either synaptically by repetitive stimulation of MFs (tetanus) or by direct elevation of cAMP by the application of the adenylyl cyclase (AC) activator, forskolin.
source: MF-LTP can be induced either synaptically by repetitive stimulation of MFs (tetanus) or by direct elevation of cAMP by the application of the adenylyl cyclase (AC) activator, forskolin.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: Previous studies using mice with defects in specific cyclases or subunits of PKA have suggested mechanistic differences in synaptic versus forskolin-induced LTP in the MF pathway.
source: Previous studies using mice with defects in specific cyclases or subunits of PKA have suggested mechanistic differences in synaptic versus forkolin-induced LTP in this pathway (Huang et al., 1995; Wong et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated with citations to Huang et al., 1995 and Wong et al., 1999.

claim: The role of sub-cellular localization of the cAMP/PKA signaling pathway has not been addressed in DGCs.
source: The role of sub-cellular localization of the cAMP/PKA signaling pathway has not been addressed in DGCs and could play a critical role in both synaptic plasticity and contextual discrimination.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Sub-cellular localization of the cAMP/PKA signaling pathway could play a critical role in both synaptic plasticity and contextual discrimination.
source: The role of sub-cellular localization of the cAMP/PKA signaling pathway has not been addressed in DGCs and could play a critical role in both synaptic plasticity and contextual discrimination.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential importance.
